profile.name: do-si-do
profile.tagline: A circular dance move where partners pass back-to-back without turning to face each other.
profile.insight: Do-si-do involves dancers passing right shoulders, moving back-to-back, then passing left shoulders to return, all without turning to face each other.
profile.profile: Do-si-do is a dance move used in square dance, contra dance, English country dance, and Scottish country dance. Two dancers face each other, advance passing right shoulders, move back-to-back passing behind each other, then pass left shoulders to return to start. The move typically takes 6–8 counts and requires spatial awareness. Variations include left shoulder passes and fractional dosados. Styling flourishes like the Hungarian Swing add arm and body movements without extending the move's duration.
profile.profile_long:
Do-si-do, also spelled dosado, do-se-do, or dos-à-dos, is a fundamental dance move found in several social dance forms including square dance, contra dance, English country dance, and Scottish country dance. The term originates from the French phrase dos-à-dos, meaning 'back to back,' which accurately describes the movement where two dancers pass around each other without turning to face one another. The dancers begin facing each other and advance by passing right shoulders, then each moves to the right passing behind the other dancer, resulting in a back-to-back position. They then move backward passing left shoulders to return to their original positions. This circular movement typically takes 6 to 8 counts to complete and requires coordination and spatial awareness between partners.

The basic footwork involves advancing forward to pass right shoulders, sidestepping behind the partner, and retreating to pass left shoulders. Depending on the dance style and space, dancers may adjust their shoulders diagonally to reduce lateral movement. Variations include starting with left shoulder passes, known as 'left do-si-do,' 'do-si-don't,' or 'reverse do-si-do.' Fractional dosados such as 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 dosados result in dancers standing side-by-side or back-to-back, often joining hands to form waves of varying sizes.

Styling flourishes vary locally; a common embellishment is the 'Hungarian Swing' or 'Highland Fling' styling where dancers momentarily stop hip-to-hip, link arms in a Highland Fling pose, pivot 360 degrees on the balls of their feet, then release and face each other again. In contra dance, experienced dancers may add counterclockwise turns while circling. Women may perform skirtwork by moving their skirts side to side during shoulder passes, while men might place arms atop each other reminiscent of Russian folk dance.

The spelling varies by tradition: 'do-si-do' is common in English dictionaries and contra dance, 'dosado' or 'DoSaDo' is used in modern western square dance, and 'dos-à-dos' remains in Scottish country dance. In English country dance, the move is called 'back to back.' The move is social and non-sacred, performed in community dance settings. It is not restricted or ritualistic.

The do-si-do is a foundational figure that connects various folk and social dances across regions, emphasizing partner coordination and spatial navigation without direct eye contact during the move. It is often taught as an essential step in square dance and contra dance classes and is a building block for more complex figures and styling.

sections.origins_and_history: The do-si-do derives from the French term dos-à-dos meaning 'back to back.' It is a dance move incorporated into multiple social dance traditions such as square dance, contra dance, English country dance, and Scottish country dance. Its presence in these diverse forms indicates its role as a basic partner interaction figure in Western social dance history.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Two dancers face each other and advance passing right shoulders. Without turning, each moves to the right passing behind the other, resulting in a back-to-back position. Then moving backward, they pass left shoulders to return to their starting places. The move usually takes 6 to 8 counts. Variations include starting with left shoulders or fractional dosados ending side-by-side or back-to-back. Styling may include skirtwork for women and arm positions for men, or a 360° pivot in the Hungarian Swing style. Technique is based on spatial awareness and smooth circular movement without turning to face the partner.
sections.costume_and_setting: Women may move skirts side to side during the move, indicating the use of skirts in some traditions. Men may adopt arm positions similar to Russian folk dance. The move is performed in social dance settings such as square dance halls, contra dance events, and country dance gatherings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Do-si-do is a social dance figure used in community dances and social gatherings. It is not sacred or ritualistic. It fosters coordination and interaction between dance partners.
sections.regional_variants: The spelling and some stylistic elements vary by region and dance tradition: 'do-si-do' in contra dance and English dictionaries; 'dosado' or 'DoSaDo' in modern western square dance; 'dos-à-dos' in Scottish country dance; 'back to back' in English country dance. Variations include left shoulder passes, fractional dosados, and styling flourishes like the Hungarian Swing.
sections.lineage: Do-si-do is a basic dance step (dance move) with roots in French social dance terminology and incorporated into various Western social dance forms including square dance, contra dance, English country dance, and Scottish country dance.

profile.era: 19th century or earlier (exact era not specified in sources)
profile.country: France (origin of term), widely used in USA, UK, Scotland

basic_steps: Move to your right passing behind your partner back-to-back.
Return to your original position facing your partner.
teaching.formation: Performed by two dancers facing each other.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with basic right shoulder pass and back-to-back movement; styling and fractional dosados are advanced variations.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, facing partner at start; maintain orientation facing same direction throughout move.
movement_profile.footwork: Advance passing right shoulders, sidestep right behind partner, retreat passing left shoulders; smooth circular motion without turning to face partner.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Typically relaxed; women may move skirts side to side; men may place arms atop each other; styling includes arm holds for Hungarian Swing.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Hips pass close but without turning; torso faces same direction throughout.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Two dancers facing each other; space permitting slight diagonal shoulder adjustment to reduce lateral movement.
movement_profile.partnering: No hand holds during basic move; styling may include hand holds or arm links.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Moderate tempo, steady counts to complete move in 6–8 beats.

signature_moves.name: Hungarian Swing
signature_moves.description: At right hip-to-right hip, link right hands on waists, lift left arms overhead, pivot 360° together on balls of feet.

movement_profile.difficulty: Beginner to intermediate depending on styling.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid turning to face partner during the move; avoid rushing the counts; respect space to prevent collisions.

episode_brief.title_hook: Do-si-do: The Back-to-Back Dance Move That Connects Traditions
episode_brief.logline: Explore the do-si-do, a circular dance move linking dancers without turning to face each other, central to square and contra dance.
beats: Introduction to the term do-si-do and its French origin dos-à-dos.
Demonstration of the basic do-si-do step with two dancers.
Explanation of the right shoulder pass, back-to-back movement, and left shoulder pass.
Showcase of styling variations like skirtwork and the Hungarian Swing.
Discussion of fractional dosados and their hand waves.
Comparison of spelling and usage in different dance traditions.
Interview with a square dance caller explaining the move's role.
Closing with a group do-si-do in a social dance setting.

drills: Practice facing a partner and passing right shoulders.
Complete the full do-si-do in 6–8 counts.
Practice skirtwork for women and arm positions for men.
Try 1/4 and 1/2 dosado positions and hand waves.
Add counterclockwise turns during the do-si-do.
Practice transitions into and out of do-si-do.

visual_motifs: Close-up of dancers passing right shoulders without turning.
Hands linked in Highland Fling pose during Hungarian Swing.
Group waves formed by joined hands.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: Experienced square dance caller with clear, friendly teaching style and knowledge of dance history.
episode_brief.music_cue: Moderate tempo folk or square dance tune with steady beat.

claims.text: Do-si-do , also spelled dosado, do-se-do, or dos-à-dos, is a dance move found in several forms of social dance, including square dance, contra dance, English country dance, and Scottish country dance.
claims.quote: Do-si-do , also spelled dosado, do-se-do, or dos-à-dos, is a dance move found in several forms of social dance, including square dance, contra dance, English country dance, and Scottish country dance.

claims.text: The move involves two dancers approaching each other, passing around one another back-to-back, and returning to their original positions without turning to face each other during the maneuver.
claims.quote: The move involves two dancers approaching each other, passing around one another back-to-back, and returning to their original positions without turning to face each other during the maneuver.

claims.text: It is a circular movement where two people, who are initially facing each other, walk around each other without or almost without turning, i.e., facing in the same direction (same wall) all the time.
claims.quote: It is a circular movement where two people, who are initially facing each other, walk around each other without or almost without turning, i.e., facing in the same direction (same wall) all the time.

claims.text: In most cases it takes 6–8 counts to complete.
claims.quote: In most cases it takes 6–8 counts to complete.

claims.text: Dancers advance and pass right shoulders, without turning each dancer moves to the right passing in back of the other dancer. At this moment the partners face away from each other, then moving backwards dancers pass left shoulders returning to starting position.
claims.quote: dancers advance and pass right shoulders, without turning each dancer moves to the right passing in back of the other dancer. At this moment the partners face away from each other, then moving backwards dancers pass left shoulders returning to starting position.

claims.text: The advancing pass may also be by the left shoulders, although it may be called as a 'left do-si-do', 'see-saw', 'do-si-don't', or 'reverse do-si-do'.
claims.quote: The advancing pass may also be by the left shoulders, although it may be called as a 'left do-si-do', 'see-saw', 'do-si-don't', or 'reverse do-si-do'.

claims.text: While executing this move, women may move their skirts with their hands from side to side (skirtwork), flaring it to the right as right shoulders pass, and to the left as left shoulders pass. Men may decide to place their arms on top of each other, in a style very similar to Russian folk dancing.
claims.quote: While executing this move, women may move their skirts with their hands from side to side (skirtwork), flaring it to the right as right shoulders pass, and to the left as left shoulders pass. Men may decide to place their arms on top of each other, in a style very similar to Russian folk dancing.

claims.text: The term is a corruption of the original French term dos-à-dos for the dance move, which means 'back to back', as opposed to 'vis-à-vis' which means 'face to face'.
claims.quote: The term is a corruption of the original French term dos-à-dos for the dance move, which means 'back to back', as opposed to 'vis-à-vis' which means 'face to face'.

claims.text: Do-si-do is the most common spelling in modern English dictionaries and is the spelling used in contra dance, sometimes without hyphens.
claims.quote: Do-si-do is the most common spelling in modern English dictionaries and is the spelling used in contra dance, sometimes without hyphens.

claims.text: In modern western square dancing, the usual spelling is Dosado which is the closest to the original French form as it’s pronounced in French [Dozado] (used by Callerlab, the largest international association of square dance callers) or DoSaDo (used by the American Callers Association).
claims.quote: In modern western square dancing, the usual spelling is Dosado which is the closest to the original French form as it’s pronounced in French [Dozado] (used by Callerlab, the largest international association of square dance callers) or DoSaDo (used by the American Callers Association).

claims.text: Dos-à-dos is still in current use in some dance traditions, such as Scottish country dance.
claims.quote: Dos-à-dos is still in current use in some dance traditions, such as Scottish country dance.

claims.text: In English country dance and other British dance forms, it is known as the 'back to back'.
claims.quote: In English country dance and other British dance forms, it is known as the 'back to back'.

claims.text: Styling traditions, or the addition of flourishes to a basic step, tend to be local, and not all dancers like to do styling, but nevertheless a common styling done to the dosado is the 'Hungarian Swing' or 'Highland Fling' styling.
claims.quote: Styling traditions, or the addition of flourishes to a basic step, tend to be local, and not all dancers like to do styling, but nevertheless a common styling done to the dosado is the 'Hungarian Swing' or 'Highland Fling' styling.

claims.text: The two people, who are initially facing each other, step forward as if they will pass each other by the right shoulder (as in a normal Dosado), but they stop momentarily when they are right hip-to-right hip, stretch right arms across each other and place right hands on each other's waist, simultaneously they lift left arms up with left hands above their own heads, in what is perceived as a 'Highland Fling' position, then pivot around 360° together, rotating on the balls of their inner feet.
claims.quote: The two people, who are initially facing each other, step forward as if they will pass each other by the right shoulder (as in a normal Dosado), but they stop momentarily when they are right hip-to-right hip They stretch right arms across each other and place right hands on each other's waist, simultaneously they lift left arms up with left hands above their own heads, in what is perceived as a 'Highland Fling' position They pivot around 360° together, rotating on the balls of their inner feet

claims.text: Even with styling the move should take no longer to execute than a normal Dosado.
claims.quote: Even with styling the move should take no longer to execute than a normal Dosado.

claims.text: In contra dance it is common for experienced dancers to embellish the move by making one or more counterclockwise turns as they go around the other dancer.
claims.quote: In contra dance it is common for experienced dancers to embellish the move by making one or more counterclockwise turns as they go around the other dancer.

claims.text: The Dosado can also be fractionalized—⁠1/4⁠ Dosado results in the active dancers standing side-by-side right hip-to-right hip, ⁠1/2⁠ Dosado results in the active dancers standing back-to-back, and ⁠3/4⁠ Dosado results in the active dancers standing side-by-side left hip-to-left hip.
claims.quote: The Dosado can also be fractionalized—⁠1/4⁠ Dosado results in the active dancers standing side-by-side right hip-to-right hip, ⁠1/2⁠ Dosado results in the active dancers standing back-to-back, and ⁠3/4⁠ Dosado results in the active dancers standing side-by-side left hip-to-left hip.

claims.text: When standing side-to-side the dancers join adjacent hands palm-to-palm to make a mini-wave (in the case of two people), an ocean wave (in the case of three-six people), or a tidal wave (in the case of eight people).
claims.quote: When standing side-to-side the dancers join adjacent hands palm-to-palm to make a mini-wave (in the case of two people), an ocean wave (in the case of three-six people), or a tidal wave (in the case of eight people).

claims.text: A Dosado 1½ consists of performing a full Dosado followed by an additional half Dosado, typically resulting in the dancers ending back-to-back.
claims.quote: A Dosado 1½ consists of performing a full Dosado followed by an additional half Dosado, typically resulting in the dancers ending back-to-back.

claims.text: Such variations are often regarded as entertaining 'gimmicks' within modern square dance communities.
claims.quote: Such variations are often regarded as entertaining 'gimmicks' within modern square dance communities.

claims.text: El do-si-do, también llamado dosado, do-se-do o dos-à-dos, es un paso de baile presente en diversas formas de baile social, como el square dance, la contradanza, el baile country inglés y el baile country escocés.
claims.quote: El do-si-do, también llamado dosado, do-se-do o dos-à-dos, es un paso de baile presente en diversas formas de baile social, como el square dance, la contradanza, el baile country inglés y el baile country escocés.

claims.text: El paso consiste en que dos bailarines se acerquen, uno alrededor del otro, espalda con espalda, y regresen a sus posiciones originales sin girarse para mirarse durante el paso.
claims.quote: El paso consiste en que dos bailarines se acerquen, uno alrededor del otro, espalda con espalda, y regresen a sus posiciones originales sin girarse para mirarse durante el paso.

claims.text: Requiere coordinación y percepción espacial entre los participantes.
claims.quote: Requiere coordinación y percepción espacial entre los participantes.

claims.text: Es un movimiento circular en el que dos personas, inicialmente mirándose cara a cara, caminan una alrededor de la otra sin apenas girarse, es decir, mirando siempre en la misma dirección.
claims.quote: Es un movimiento circular en el que dos personas, inicialmente mirándose cara a cara, caminan una alrededor de la otra sin apenas girarse, es decir, mirando siempre en la misma dirección.

claims.text: En la mayoría de los casos, se completa en 6 u 8 tiempos.
claims.quote: En la mayoría de los casos, se completa en 6 u 8 tiempos.

claims.text: Los bailarines avanzan y pasan los hombros derechos, sin girar cada bailarín se mueve hacia la derecha pasando por detrás del otro.
claims.quote: Los bailarines avanzan y pasan los hombros derechos, sin girar cada bailarín se mueve hacia la derecha pasando por detrás del otro.

claims.text: En ese momento, los bailarines miran a direcciones opuestas. Luego, moviéndose hacia atrás, los bailarines pasan el hombro izquierdo y regresan a la posición inicial.
claims.quote: En ese momento, los bailarines miran a direcciones opuestas. Luego, moviéndose hacia atrás, los bailarines pasan el hombro izquierdo y regresan a la posición inicial.

claims.text: El pase de avance también puede hacerse por los hombros izquierdos, pudiendo llamarse «do-si-do izquierdo», «do-si-no» o «do-si-do inverso».
claims.quote: El pase de avance también puede hacerse por los hombros izquierdos, pudiendo llamarse «do-si-do izquierdo», «do-si-no» o «do-si-do inverso».

claims.text: Al ejecutar este movimiento, las mujeres pueden mover la falda con las manos de un lado a otro, abriéndola hacia la derecha al pasar el hombro derecho y hacia la izquierda al pasar el izquierdo.
claims.quote: Al ejecutar este movimiento, las mujeres pueden mover la falda con las manos de un lado a otro, abriéndola hacia la derecha al pasar el hombro derecho y hacia la izquierda al pasar el izquierdo.

claims.text: Los hombres pueden colocar los brazos uno sobre el otro, en un estilo muy similar al de la danza folclórica rusa.
claims.quote: Los hombres pueden colocar los brazos uno sobre el otro, en un estilo muy similar al de la danza folclórica rusa.

claims.text: El término es una derivación del término francés original dos-à-dos para el movimiento de baile, que significa «espalda con espalda», en oposición a «vis-à-vis» que significa 'cara a cara'.
claims.quote: El término es una derivación del término francés original dos-à-dos para el movimiento de baile, que significa «espalda con espalda», en oposición a «vis-à-vis» que significa 'cara a cara'.

claims.text: En el baile occidental moderno, la ortografía habitual es «Dosado», siendo más cercano a la forma francesa original tal como se pronuncia en francés o DoSaDo (utilizado por la Asociación Americana de Locutores).
claims.quote: En el baile occidental moderno, la ortografía habitual es «Dosado», siendo más cercano a la forma francesa original tal como se pronuncia en francés o DoSaDo (utilizado por la Asociación Americana de Locutores).

claims.text: El dos-à-dos todavía se usa actualmente en algunas tradiciones de danza, como la danza campestre escocesa.
claims.quote: El dos-à-dos todavía se usa actualmente en algunas tradiciones de danza, como la danza campestre escocesa.

claims.text: Un estilo común para el dosado es el «Swing húngaro» o «danza de las tierras latas escocesas».
claims.quote: Un estilo común para el dosado es el «Swing húngaro» o «danza de las tierras latas escocesas».

claims.text: En cualquier caso, el movimiento no debería tardar más en ejecutarse que un dosado normal.
claims.quote: En cualquier caso, el movimiento no debería tardar más en ejecutarse que un dosado normal.

claims.text: El dosado también se puede fraccionar, el primer cuarto del dosado da como resultado que los bailarines activos se paren uno al lado del otro, cadera derecha con cadera derecha, el segundo cuarto del dosado da como resultado que los bailarines activos se paren espalda con espalda y el tercer cuarto uno al lado del otro, con la cadera izquierda contra la izquierda.
claims.quote: El dosado también se puede fraccionar, el primer cuarto del dosado da como resultado que los bailarines activos se paren uno al lado del otro, cadera derecha con cadera derecha, el segundo cuarto del dosado da como resultado que los bailarines activos se paren espalda con espalda y el tercer cuarto uno al lado del otro, con la cadera izquierda contra la izquierda.

claims.text: Al hacerlo, unen las manos adyacentes, palma con palma, para formar una ola.
claims.quote: Al hacerlo, unen las manos adyacentes, palma con palma, para formar una ola.

claims.text: Un dosado 1½ consiste en realizar un dosado completo seguido de medio dosado adicional, lo que generalmente resulta en que los bailarines terminen uno tras otro.
claims.quote: Un dosado 1½ consiste en realizar un dosado completo seguido de medio dosado adicional, lo que generalmente resulta en que los bailarines terminen uno tras otro.

claims.text: Estas variaciones suelen considerarse trucos entretenidos en las comunidades de baile moderno.
claims.quote: Estas variaciones suelen considerarse trucos entretenidos en las comunidades de baile moderno.
